questions.q: How can I tell if an AI tool is good for my business?
questions.a: Good AI saves time and money, ties to outcomes you already track, works with your existing systems and improves over time. If a tool meets those tests, it's likely worth the investment. If it creates extra work or can't explain what it's doing, it probably isn't.

questions.q: What are the signs of bad AI in a restaurant?
questions.a: Bad AI creates more work than it saves, because your team keeps checking or redoing its output. It lacks context, so it might suggest irrelevant upsells or misread a guest's sentiment. It's also often a black box that doesn't adapt, which makes staff stop trusting and using it.

questions.q: What questions should I ask before buying an AI tool?
questions.a: Ask whether it reduces your workload or just moves it around, and whether you can tie it to a clear outcome like speed, revenue, retention or accuracy. Check that it plugs into the tools you already use. Finally, consider whether your team will actually trust it and use it day to day.

questions.q: Why does AI need to integrate with my other systems?
questions.a: Without access to customer history, inventory or sales data, AI is guessing. Integration gives it the context to make accurate, relevant decisions, such as replying to a review with the right details. It also means the tool fits into how your team already works.

questions.q: Does voice AI work in restaurant drive-thrus?
questions.a: It can, when it's built for the job. Well-designed drive-thru voice AI pulls in order history, adjusts menus by time of day and learns from every transaction. Generic voice assistants without that context tend to mishear guests and cause frustration, especially when they can't hand off to a person.
